findings.title: markAcked — the round-10 'the server has seen this id' fact — is earned from documents the server has NOT acknowledged (query snapshots are latency-compensated)
findings.trace: FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-77 builds CloudRead from `snapshot.metadata.isFromCache` only; per-document `document.metadata.hasPendingWrites` is discarded (CloudRead has no per-row provenance, DropStore.swift:50-53). DropStore.swift:503 sets cloudReadServerServed=!servedFromCache, then :508 `if cloudReadServerServed { markAcked(drop.id) }` for EVERY returned row, persisting to UserDefaults key ackedCloudDropIDs (:397,1006-1010). Firestore merges the local mutation queue into server-served query results, so a staged-but-unacked write appears in a snapshot whose metadata.isFromCache is false. I REPRODUCED this against the Firestore emulator (temp probe, since removed): after staging 400 writes offline and re-enabling the network, `getDocs` returned `fromCache = false` with 397 of 401 documents carrying `hasPendingWrites = true`. This is exactly the snapshot refresh() marks acked. The same file's sibling read paths do check per-document provenance — ReactionService.swift:183 and AccountService.swift:61-62 — so the omission is inconsistent, not a considered trade.
findings.harm: Fabricated positive evidence produces a PERMANENT false data-loss alarm — the exact round-9 seams-1/lens-3 blocker, re-entered through a new door. Trigger: user creates a drop offline (add() → DropStore.swift:712 → FirestoreAcked deadline → ackTimedOut → stays pendingSyncIDs, never acked); connectivity returns; the app foregrounds and refresh() runs (RootView.swift:164 / MapScreen.swift:106 / DropsListScreen.swift:26) while the queued create is still in flight → the row is in the server-served snapshot → markAcked, durably. The staged write is then permanently refused (gRPC 16 unauthenticated after a token-refresh failure, or 3 invalid-argument) so no server copy ever exists. The user deletes the drop; under the LIVE v2 ruleset a delete of an absent doc DENIES (pinned, deployed-rules.test.mjs:53) → three refusals → DropStore.swift:943 sees the fabricated acked fact → markUnresolvedDelete → ProfileScreen.swift:98 shows 'N deletions couldn't finish — the cloud copy may still exist'. It can never clear: retirement needs serverConfirmsAbsent, gated on knownAbsenceCapability == .answers (DropStore.swift:593), and under v2 probeAbsenceCapability returns .denied (FirebaseDropStore.swift:206-208, pinned deployed-rules.test.mjs:49). Permanent alarm about a cloud copy that never existed, until the Wave-A v3 deploy.
findings.fix: Make CloudRead carry per-row provenance and let only server-confirmed rows earn the acked fact. Minimal shape: add `var serverConfirmedIDs: Set<UUID>` to CloudRead (DropStore.swift:50-53); in FirebaseDropStore.loadDropsWithProvenance (:67-77) populate it from `document.metadata.hasPendingWrites == false` while still merging every row for display; change DropStore.swift:508 to `if cloudReadServerServed, read.serverConfirmedIDs.contains(drop.id) { markAcked(drop.id) }`. Update GatedCloudStore (DropStoreTests.swift:1034-1038) to express the case, per binding rule 6.

findings.title: The delete pipeline has no refusal taxonomy: transient/quota errors spend the 3-attempt budget, permanently abandoning the delete and (when acked) raising an alarm that can never retire
findings.trace: performCloudDelete's catch-all (DropStore.swift:924-948) treats EVERY thrown error as a refusal: attempts+=1 at :937, and at :940 `attempts >= 3` clears the tombstone and either markUnresolvedDelete (:944) or resolves silently (:946). The save path does classify — FirebaseDropStore.swift:131-133 uses DropStoreError.terminalRefusalReason, whose taxonomy (:230-246) explicitly keeps gRPC 4/8/10/13/14 RETRYABLE, pinned by RefusalTaxonomyTests (DropStoreTests.swift:944-153 for codes 4,8,10,13,14). FirebaseDropStore.delete (:162-171) rethrows the raw rejection with no classification, so the delete pipeline sees a transient code and a permission-denied identically. Once an id moves to unresolvedDeleteIDs it is never retried again: reconcileCloud replays only pendingDeleteIDs (DropStore.swift:794-797). deleteAttempts is in-memory (:381), so three refusals within one session is the whole budget, and reconcileCloud() fires from every refresh (DropStore.swift:575).
findings.harm: Silent, permanent loss of a delete intent plus an un-clearable false alarm — both charter violations. Trigger: the Firestore project hits its Spark daily write quota (or any RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED / UNAUTHENTICATED window on a flaky connection). The user deletes a shared drop. Three refreshes during that window (foreground, map pan, pull-to-refresh) spend all three attempts on errors that would have succeeded an hour later. If the id was acked, ProfileScreen.swift:98 shows 'the cloud copy may still exist' forever (retirement is capability-gated to .answers, unreachable under the live v2 rules) AND the delete is never retried — the drop's magic link keeps working for every recipient, permanently. If the id was never acked, DropStore.swift:946 logs and resolves as DONE with no surface at all, so a surviving cloud copy is reported as a completed deletion.
findings.fix: Classify delete rejections with the taxonomy that already exists. In performCloudDelete, before spending an attempt: `guard DropStoreError.terminalRefusalReason(error) != nil else { return }` (transient → tombstone stays pending, no attempt spent, reconcileCloud retries), and only count genuine non-retryable refusals toward the bound. Separately, persist deleteAttempts alongside the tombstone so the budget is a real lifetime bound rather than a per-session one, and make the never-acked 'resolved DONE' path leave an observable record instead of only a log line.

findings.title: A cache-served cloud read revokes a server-issued sync-failure verdict (`lastSyncError = nil`) — the provenance flag needed to prevent it is computed 11 lines above and unused here
findings.trace: refresh() computes cloudReadServerServed at DropStore.swift:503 and spends it on the evidence latch (:569) and markAcked (:508), but the success path unconditionally clears the error at :514 — inside a `do` block whose read (FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-66, default source) returns cached results without throwing when the device is offline. lastSyncError is set only by a real server answer at :519. Consumers: ProfileScreen.swift:127 ('Sync issue — …' rung) and DropsListScreen.swift:48 (icloud.slash banner). Binding rules 3 and 4: the verdict's producing condition (the server's refusal) has not disappeared, and a local cache hit is not its issuing authority.
findings.harm: The user's only signal that their drops are not reaching the cloud disappears exactly when they can least afford to lose it. Trigger: a server-answered read failure (permission-denied from App Check enforcement, an expired/revoked token, or a post-v3-deploy query-shape mismatch) sets 'Sync issue — …'. The user walks into a subway / enables airplane mode; the next refresh is served from the Firestore cache, does not throw, and nils the error. Both surfaces go quiet and the ProfileScreen ladder falls through to 'Checking sync status…' or, if evidence was already latched, 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops', while the account is still refused by the backend.
findings.fix: Gate the clear on the same provenance the latch uses: `if cloudReadServerServed { lastSyncError = nil }` at DropStore.swift:514. A cache-served read leaves the prior server verdict standing, which is what binding rule 4 requires.

findings.title: fetchSharedDrop returns the same `nil` for 'the server said not-there', 'we never asked anyone', and 'the document exists but did not decode' — and round 10 turned that nil into a causal, non-retryable expiry verdict
findings.trace: Round 10 (flows-6) redefined the contract at DropSharingService.swift:48-51: nil == the server answered 'gone', throw == unreachable. Three producers of nil remain: :53 `guard AppConfig.firebaseConfigured else { return nil }` — nothing was asked (AppConfig.swift:13-14 makes this a supported no-plist mode); :57 `guard snapshot.exists` — the only honest server answer; :71 `guard var cloud = try? snapshot.data(as: CloudDrop.self) else { return nil }` — the document EXISTS but the envelope decode threw (the inner `drop` key is `try c.decode`, not decodeIfPresent, at :67, and GeoDrop's field decodes still throw on type mismatch, GeoDrop.swift:105-125). ReceiveScreen.swift:147-151 maps nil → .gone, and :114-123 renders 'This drop isn't available' / 'The sender may have taken it back, or the link expired' with NO retry button (:124 gates Try-again to .unreachable only). Symmetrically, a rules DENIAL (a link to a still-private drop, pinned as denying at rules.test.mjs:69) throws and is rendered as 'You seem to be offline' — a fabricated diagnosis in the other direction.
findings.harm: A recipient is told a live gift expired, with no way to retry. Trigger (decode): the live v2 ruleset lets any signed-in user overwrite any drop document (pinned as still-present, deployed-rules.test.mjs:61), so one malformed or hijacked write turns every recipient's magic link into a permanent 'the link expired' — the sender sees a healthy synced drop and the recipient sees an expiry that never happened. Trigger (not-configured): any build or config state without GoogleService-Info.plist reports every magic link as expired rather than 'cloud is off'. Both are fabricated negative verdicts produced by a fallthrough, violating binding rule 1.
findings.fix: Return a three-valued result — `enum SharedDropFetch { case found(GeoDrop); case absent; case unknown(reason) }`. Only `snapshot.exists == false` yields .absent; the not-configured guard, the decode failure, and a permission-denied all yield .unknown. ReceiveScreen renders .unknown with the retryable copy and drops the causal 'the link expired' claim from anything but .absent.

findings.title: The drift lock covers only the emoji list; the v3 reaction key allow-list is not locked to DropReaction's encoded fields, and the rules suite hardcodes the same keys — so both 'sides' can drift from the app together
findings.trace: drift-check.mjs:13-28 parses exactly two things: ReactionSession.reactions (Sharing/ReactionSession.swift:21) and the `data.emoji in [...]` list in firestore.rules:77. The other client-coupled clause — `request.resource.data.keys().hasOnly(['id','emoji','uid','byName','at'])` at firestore.rules:78 — is checked only by rules.test.mjs, whose payload helper (:96-98) hardcodes the same five keys rather than deriving them from the Swift type. The actual contract is DropReaction's synthesized encoding (ReactionService.swift:10-16), written through FirestoreAcked.setData at :59-64. Nothing connects those three lists.
findings.harm: A future one-line change to DropReaction silently breaks every reaction after the v3 deploy, with both emulator suites still green. Trigger: someone adds a field (client version, drop id, a `seenAt`) to DropReaction; the encoded document then has 6 keys; hasOnly fails; every send is permission-denied → ReactionService.send throws at :70-73 → the viewer's reaction renders as failed on MemoryScreen and the sender's toast never fires. The v2 rules currently in production have no key restriction (firestore.rules.deployed:39-40), so the breakage appears only at the moment of the v3 deploy — the worst possible time to discover it. This is precisely the class of drift the emoji lock exists to prevent.
findings.fix: Extend drift-check.mjs with a `reactionKeys()` pair: parse the property names of `struct DropReaction` from ReactionService.swift and the `keys().hasOnly([...])` list from firestore.rules, and fail on any mismatch; then have rules.test.mjs build its reaction payload from the parsed list (as it already does for emoji via appEmojiList()) instead of a hardcoded literal.

findings.title: The absence-capability latch is process-lifetime and never re-armed: one non-rules permission-denied disables all tombstone retirement for the whole app run, and a v3 deploy is not picked up until relaunch
findings.trace: DropStore.swift:586-592 probes only when knownAbsenceCapability == nil and latches any non-.inconclusive answer for the lifetime of the DropLibrary (created once per app process, DropStore.swift:405-425). accountDidChange() (:642-651) resets hasCompletedCleanRefresh but not knownAbsenceCapability. FirebaseDropStore.probeAbsenceCapability (:198-212) maps ANY FirestoreErrorCode.permissionDenied to .denied — including denials that are not about absent-document semantics (App Check enforcement, a revoked/expired ID token, a project-wide rules lockdown). The gate at :593 then skips every retirement probe. Correctly, the probe itself is sound and side-effect-free under both rulesets: v2 denies a random-UUID get (verified, deployed-rules.test.mjs:49) and v3 answers it (verified, rules.test.mjs:63), and a random UUID cannot exist so the `.answers` branch cannot be fabricated by a hit.
findings.harm: Tombstones and 'the cloud copy may still exist' alarms (ProfileScreen.swift:98) stay stuck for the session even after the condition that produced them is gone. Trigger A: a transient App Check / token failure during the one probe of a session latches .denied; retirement is dead until the user force-quits, so deletes that the server has in fact completed keep showing the alarm. Trigger B: after the Wave-A v3 deploy, a long-lived session that latched .denied before the deploy never re-probes, so no tombstone retires until relaunch.
findings.fix: Give .denied a bounded life: re-probe when the latched value is .denied and either the session has crossed a refresh threshold or accountDidChange() fired (reset knownAbsenceCapability there alongside hasCompletedCleanRefresh). Optionally distinguish rules-denial from auth/App-Check denial by probing a path the rules always permit for the signed-in user (users/{uid}) before concluding .denied.

cleanAreas: FirestoreAcked.race — all four stream endings verified honest: a yielded ack → .acked (FirestoreAcked.swift:85), a thrown finish → .rejected via the group rethrow at :98/:105, the deadline → .queuedLocally (:94-97), and BOTH cancellation and a no-yield finish → .queuedLocally (:86-92, :102). FirestoreAckedTests.swift:11-71 covers all four non-vacuously. Residual, not a finding: a server answer that arrives AFTER the deadline is delivered into an abandoned continuation and dropped, so a permanently-refused write reads as 'Still uploading' (ShareDropSheet.swift:147) until reconcileCloud() re-issues it — which every refresh does (DropStore.swift:575; RootView.swift:164, MapScreen.swift:106, DropsListScreen.swift:26), so it self-heals.

FirestoreAcked.setData's staging path — AsyncThrowingStream's build closure is non-escaping and runs synchronously, so `stagingError` is genuinely observable at FirestoreAcked.swift:53. An encoder throw is a rejection, never a queue; the write is never reported as staged when it was not.

Snapshot-level `isFromCache` IS the correct provenance signal for getDocuments — verified on the emulator: an offline read reports fromCache=true and an online read false. The defect (lens-1) is only the discarding of per-DOCUMENT provenance, not the choice of signal.

probeAbsenceCapability is sound and side-effect-free under BOTH rulesets. Verified by running both suites: v2 denies a random-UUID get (deployed-rules.test.mjs:49) and v3 answers it (rules.test.mjs:63); a random UUID cannot exist, so the `.answers` branch can never be reached by a hit; @firebase/rules-unit-testing's assertFails only accepts permission-denied errors, so the FirebaseDropStore.swift:206-208 error mapping is genuinely pinned by those assertions. The probe writes nothing.

ackedCloudIDs under a uid change is NOT wrong in the dangerous direction: an id acked under uid A whose cloud copy becomes undeletable under a new uid B correctly raises the alarm, because the copy really does survive (FirebaseDropStore.swift:153's owner backstop is bypassed by the ghost drop at DropStore.swift:911-912, so a real delete is issued and honestly refused). A TTL'd or externally-deleted server copy also resolves correctly — Firestore deletes are idempotent, so the delete acks and clearAcked fires at DropStore.swift:918.

Both emulator suites execute and pass on this machine (npm test with /opt/homebrew/opt/openjdk on PATH; the default PATH lacks Java, which is why the suite cannot run unattended here — CI is a recorded residual). 28 v3 assertions + 5 deployed-v2 assertions + the emoji drift lock, all green. Every client call shape I traced is covered by or consistent with the v3 rules: the owner-scoped list (FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-66 vs rules.test.mjs:73), the magic-link get (DropSharingService.swift:54-56 vs :71), the absent-doc get both ways, merge-setData as create-then-update (FirebaseDropStore.swift:116-119 under firestore.rules:59-64), absent delete, the reactions order+limit list, and the own users/{uid} get.

DropSharingService's server-sourced fetch uses getDocument(source: .server) (DropSharingService.swift:56), so a cached miss can never manufacture a 'gone' verdict — the remaining problem (lens-4) is the other nil producers, not the read source.

ReactionService's recap is the model the drop read should copy: per-document hasPendingWrites filtering (:183), own-uid exclusion (:185), snapshot-level serverAnswered (:187), and errors mapped to .unavailable (:191) rather than to an empty list.

findings.title: redeem()'s pending-edit guard is structurally empty for received drops — re-opening a magic link silently destroys every local edit the recipient made
findings.trace: DropStore.swift:679 `if pendingSyncIDs.contains(drop.id) { return }` is the ONLY protection against a fetched copy overwriting the local row (:685-694 does drops[index] = drop then local.save(drop)). Population of pendingSyncIDs is exclusively via markPending (:961), whose only caller is enqueueCloudSync (:807), which returns at :809 `guard drop.receivedViaLink != true else { return }` BEFORE markPending. update() (:719-735) persists to disk at :728 and only then calls enqueueCloudSync (:734) — so a received drop's edit is durably on disk and can never be in pendingSyncIDs. The recipient reaches update() from AR: ARScreen.swift:285-286 shows adjustPanel for ANY nearest drop with no ownership gate; ARScreen.swift:484/505/526/543/593 -> GeoARSessionManager.adjustNearestDrop (:1645-1658) and relocateNearestDrop (:1822-1831) both call library.update(edited, persist: true). Re-opening the link: RootView.swift:50-54 onOpenURL -> ReceiveScreen -> onReveal -> RootView.swift:66 library.redeem(drop) with the freshly fetched server copy (DropSharingService.swift:79-81 stamps receivedViaLink = true for a drop the viewer does not own). Guard at :679 is false by construction -> overwrite. The same hole exists for terminalSyncFailureIDs rows: performCloudSync clears pending at :873/:883 and marks terminal, so a row whose edit the server REFUSED (local strictly newer than the server copy) is also unprotected, and the ShareDropSheet retry path (:205 -> retrySync(id:) -> DropStore.swift:660 resolves from live drops) then uploads the rolled-back content, destroying the edit in both places.
findings.harm: Recipient opens a link, watches the drop in AR, and uses the app's core placement affordances (height slider, size, rotation, 'Place on ground', 'Pin to a spot') to fix GPS drift and put the gift where it should be. Those edits persist to disk. The recipient later taps the same link again in iMessage (a completely normal action) — redeem() overwrites memory and disk with the sender's original coordinate/pose. All placement work is silently gone, with no error, no banner, and no undo. Owner-side variant: a drop with a terminal write verdict has its unsynced local edit replaced by the stale server copy on own-link open, and the next retry uploads the stale content permanently.
findings.fix: Stop using pendingSyncIDs as the proxy for 'the local row is authoritative'. redeem() must compare against the actual local row: load/inspect the row for drop.id and refuse the overwrite when a local row exists whose content differs and is not known-synced — i.e. when the id is in pendingSyncIDs OR in terminalSyncFailureIDs OR (drop.receivedViaLink == true and a local row already exists). Minimal correct rule for a receive: if a local row for this id already exists, keep it and only clear the tombstones/retire the delete (which is redeem's real job); insert-and-save ONLY when no local row exists. If a merge is wanted later, keep the recipient's pose fields (heightAboveGround, scale, facingDegrees, latitude, longitude) and take only sender-authored fields from the fetch.

findings.title: redeem()'s early return reports success while persisting and publishing nothing when the pending row is not loadable
findings.trace: DropStore.swift:679-684 returns with no throw and no state change, justified by the comment at :681-683 ('By the pending/tombstone invariant it was never suppressed, so it is already published'). That premise is false whenever an id is in pendingSyncIDs but has no row in `drops` — a state the library itself models and surfaces as unpushablePendingCount (:438-440) and renders in Profile/ProfileScreen.swift:112-126. pendingSyncIDs is hydrated from UserDefaults in init (:415-416) independently of any disk row, and LocalDropStore quarantine (:222-242) destroys rows while the outbox entry survives. The reap that would clear such an id runs only under `if case .clean = localOutcome` (:536) — after a quarantine the outcome is .quarantinedWholeFile then .absentFile, so the stale pending id (and therefore the dead early-return) persists across launches until some other write makes the file read clean again. RootView.swift:64-72 treats a non-throwing redeem as success and shows an error only on throw.
findings.harm: After a local-store corruption incident, the user taps a magic link for the affected drop. ReceiveScreen fetches it from the server successfully, the AR moment plays from ReactionSession's in-memory copy, and redeem() returns success — but nothing is written to disk and nothing is added to `drops`. The one recoverable copy of that drop (the server's) is refused. The drop is gone again at the next launch and the user was told nothing. Charter violation: fabricated success on a path that did nothing.
findings.fix: Make the early return conditional on the fact it claims: `if pendingSyncIDs.contains(drop.id), drops.contains(where: { $0.id == drop.id })` — otherwise fall through to the insert+save path (and clear the now-provably-stale pending id, or leave it for the reap). Alternatively have redeem() return a typed outcome (.keptLocalEdit / .stored) so the caller can distinguish 'protected your newer copy' from 'nothing happened'.

findings.title: Every launch destroys the evidence latch the auth-ready refresh just earned, suppressing the round-10 un-pushable problem rung for the whole session
findings.trace: RootView.swift:162-169 `.task(id: account.uid ?? "-")` runs `await library.refresh(near: nil)` then `library.accountDidChange()` unconditionally. Round 10's lens-4 change made accountDidChange() clear the latch: DropStore.swift:643-645 `hasCompletedCleanRefresh = false`. The task id is the uid, so it fires on the FIRST uid resolution of every launch, not only on a genuine account change — the refresh at :164 may set the latch true (DropStore.swift:569-571) and :168 immediately clears it. The only other refresh triggers are AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:34 (fires before auth, so the cloud read throws .notSignedIn at FirebaseDropStore.swift:61 and earns nothing), MapScreen.swift:105-107 (only when Explore appears / the location nil-ness flips), and the manual toolbar button DropsListScreen.swift:25-26. Round 10 introduced this by pairing a latch that is cleared on every launch (lens-4) with a failure surface newly gated behind that latch (ux-4): a real failure is now invisible where in round 9 it was visible. findings.title: Two-phase publish unconditionally destroys the published cloud half, so a superseded or failed refresh strands the library showing a false-empty list
findings.trace: DropStore.swift:473-481 publishes `drops = localOnly.values.sorted{...}` BEFORE the cloud read. Cloud rows are never persisted locally (refresh has no local.save on the merge path, :504-513), so any row that exists only in the cloud is erased from the published set at :481 and restored only if the SAME refresh reaches :527. Every mutator bumps refreshGeneration (add :702, update :720, remove :738, redeem :672, acknowledgeReadIncident :621), so any user action during the cloud read makes the in-flight refresh return at :502/:516/:518 with `drops` left at the local-only value. A cloud read failure lands the same way (:517-520 then :525-527 publishes merged == local-only). Before round 10 a superseded refresh left the PREVIOUSLY published set intact, so this class of loss did not exist; own-2 fixed the local half and opened the cloud half. Consumers: DropsListScreen.swift:83-88 renders ContentUnavailableView('No drops yet') on an empty set; MapScreen.swift:31 and HomeScreen.swift:53-59 read library.drops directly; GeoARSessionManager.swift:1242/1267 recomputes eligible/nearest drops from library.drops every tick.
findings.harm: On a reinstall/second-device account restore (local store empty, all rows in the cloud) every refresh blinks the whole library to zero: the Sent tab shows 'No drops yet — Pin your first 3D surprise' and the Map empties for the duration of the network read. If the user taps create (or any mutator fires) during that window, the superseded refresh never republishes and the entire cloud library stays invisible until another refresh completes — offline, it stays invisible indefinitely with only a small 'Sync issue' caption. The app asserts an empty library it has no evidence for.
findings.fix: Make phase 1 additive rather than authoritative: merge the freshly loaded local rows into the currently published set (keeping rows the previous completed refresh contributed) instead of replacing it — e.g. seed `localOnly` from `Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues: drops.map { ($0.id, $0) })` before overlaying the local load, then apply tombstone suppression. Better still, persist server-served cloud rows to the local store on merge so local truth is a superset and phase 1 is genuinely complete.

findings.title: Retirement probe cap prefix(5) over an unordered Set starves the tail — five permanently unretireable tombstones freeze the false 'deletions couldn't finish' alarm forever
findings.trace: DropStore.swift:584 builds `tombstones = pendingDeleteIDs.union(unresolvedDeleteIDs)` (a Set) and :594 iterates `tombstones.prefix(5)`. Set iteration order is a function of the per-process hash seed and the storage layout, so for unchanged contents it is identical on every pass within a session — the same five ids are probed every refresh and ids 6+ are never probed at all. The five leaders are only displaced when they retire (:598-607), and an id retires only when serverConfirmsAbsent returns true (FirebaseDropStore.swift:179-191). unresolvedDeleteIDs entries exist precisely because the server refused the delete three times (:940-945), i.e. the document still exists, i.e. serverConfirmsAbsent will keep returning false for them indefinitely. Five such entries permanently monopolise the cap. Any mutator bumping refreshGeneration during the loop also aborts it at :596, shortening the effective prefix further.
findings.harm: With five or more stuck tombstones (a rules misconfiguration or a stale account connection produces them in bulk), every later deletion the user performs is never verified against the server again. Profile/ProfileScreen.swift:92-102 keeps asserting 'N deletions couldn't finish — the cloud copy may still exist' for drops whose cloud copies are in fact gone, and those rows stay suppressed from the library forever — the permanent false delete alarm seams-1 was raised to eliminate, reintroduced through the cap instead of through the rules.
findings.fix: Give the probe pass a deterministic, fair order and a rotating cursor: sort the tombstones (e.g. by uuidString) into an array, keep a persisted `nextProbeIndex`, and probe five starting at the cursor, advancing it each pass so every tombstone is reached within ceil(n/5) refreshes. Prioritise unresolvedDeleteIDs (the set with a user-visible alarm attached) ahead of pendingDeleteIDs within that order.

findings.title: remove() is the only pipeline that commits a multi-step transition across an await without re-validating — a redeem landing in the local-delete window leaves the row on disk AND tombstoned
findings.trace: DropStore.swift:737-760: remove() bumps refreshGeneration at :738, suspends at :742 `try await local.delete(drop)`, then on resume unconditionally executes drops.removeAll (:748), clearPending (:752), markPendingDelete (:758) and launchCloudDelete (:759). Unlike performCloudSync (:828, :834, :872, :882, :887), performCloudDelete (:907, :915, :936) and refresh (:453, :460, :470, :502, :588, :596), it takes no generation and re-checks nothing after the await. A redeem() for the same id executing in that window runs its whole synchronous prefix (:672-689 — bumps refreshGeneration, retires the tombstones, re-writes drops[index]) and issues local.save, which the LocalDropStore actor serialises AFTER the delete, so the row is back on disk. remove() then resumes and tombstones it anyway. The markPendingDelete assert at :983 does not fire (redeem never marks pending), so nothing signals the divergence. Window = one LocalDropStore actor round-trip (whole-file read + decode + encode + atomic write), which grows with library size and with actor contention.
findings.harm: A drop the user just accepted from a link is on disk but suppressed from every surface, while the cloud delete proceeds: either the delete acks (:916-918 retires the tombstone and the drop the user deleted resurrects locally on the next refresh while its cloud copy is destroyed — a half-executed delete) or it is refused three times and the row becomes a permanent invisible on-disk orphan with a 'deletion couldn't finish' alarm. Trigger requires the redeem to land inside remove()'s disk window, so it is rare, but the outcome is silent local/cloud divergence with no surfaced verdict.
findings.fix: Give remove() the same discipline as every other pipeline: capture `let generation = refreshGeneration` after the bump at :738 and, after the await at :742, `guard refreshGeneration == generation else { return }` before mutating drops/pending/tombstone state — a redemption (or a newer remove) that superseded it then owns the outcome. If the delete must still be honoured after supersession, re-resolve the row from `drops` first and skip the tombstone when it is present.

ackedCloudIDs lifecycle — verified exact. acknowledgeReadIncident reentrancy — DropStore.swift:620-636. The synchronous clear at :622 is authoritative (the user's dismissal is not contingent on a generation), the guarded re-clear at :628 cannot re-post a warning a newer pass owns, and the refresh kick at :634 bumps its own generation at :446, so repeated taps only supersede each other. "-")` → `await library.refresh(near: nil)` (:164) → `library.accountDidChange()` (:168). refresh() earns the latch at DropStore.swift:561-571 (`hasCompletedCleanRefresh = true`); accountDidChange() unconditionally sets it back to false at DropStore.swift:645 (new in round 10, counsel lens-4) and only re-enqueues terminal ids (:646-650) — it schedules no refresh. Default tab is .home (AppRouter.swift:20). So for any user who stays on Home/You, hasCompletedCleanRefresh is false for the entire session, every session.
findings.harm: Two surfaces lie by omission. (1) ProfileScreen.swift:143-149 renders 'Checking sync status…' forever even when every drop is server-acknowledged — the 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops' rung (:150-157) is unreachable on the default path, so the app can never confirm the thing the user came to check. (2) Worse: ProfileScreen.swift:112-126 — the ux-4 rung that exists precisely to make 'N changes can't upload — the saved copy couldn't be read' visible — is gated on the same flag, so a genuine un-pushable outbox is silently downgraded to a reassuring progress message. Trigger: cold launch → anonymous sign-in lands → user taps You. Reproduces on every launch.
findings.fix: Make the account-change reset a PRECONDITION of the pass, not its epilogue: in RootView.swift:162-169 call `library.accountDidChange()` BEFORE `await library.refresh(near: nil)`, and give DropLibrary a single composed entry point (`func authDidBecomeReady() async { accountDidChange(); await refresh(near: nil) }`) so the order cannot be re-broken by a caller. Additionally add a refresh on scenePhase == .active so the latch is re-earned after backgrounding rather than depending on the user visiting Explore.

findings.title: Gone-vs-unreachable is inverted against the deployed rules: every server answer of 'not there / not yours' renders 'You seem to be offline — the surprise may still be waiting' with an endless retry, while the 'gone' verdict fires only on client-side conditions
findings.trace: ReceiveScreen.swift:144-155: `nil → failure = .gone` (:150), `catch → failure = .unreachable` (:153). DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop returns nil only for (a) `AppConfig.firebaseConfigured == false` (:53), (b) `!snapshot.exists` (:57), (c) a decode failure (:71); it throws for every rules denial. Under the ruleset round 10 itself pinned as LIVE — web/firestore.rules.deployed:35-38 evaluates `resource.data.ownerUid` on a null resource, and web/rules-tests/deployed-rules.test.mjs:49-50 asserts `absent-doc GET denies` — a deleted or expired drop returns PERMISSION_DENIED, i.e. the THROW branch. A private/unshared drop denies the same way. So (b) is unreachable in production and the honest 'gone' copy (:114-121) can be produced only by a missing plist or a schema drift, neither of which is a server verdict. The same throw path also swallows the cold-start auth race: RootView.swift:50-55 presents the sheet from `.onOpenURL`, ReceiveScreen.swift:45-50 loads immediately, while AccountService.start() (AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:31, AccountService.swift:31-40) is still awaiting signInAnonymously — request.auth == null denies under firestore.rules.deployed:35-36.
findings.harm: The product's signature flow tells the recipient the wrong thing at both ends. A recipient opening a link the sender deleted (or a private drop) is told 'Can't reach the server / You seem to be offline — the surprise may still be waiting' and given a Try again button that can never succeed — they may keep retrying, or walk to the pinned location for a drop that no longer exists. And on the very first open of a magic link from a cold launch on a slow network, a perfectly healthy link shows the same offline failure screen; the invitation only appears if the user happens to tap Try again after auth lands. Meanwhile a build with no GoogleService-Info.plist tells every recipient 'The sender may have taken it back' — a fabricated authoritative negative from a local file check.
findings.fix: Give fetchSharedDrop a three-valued result instead of Optional: `.found(GeoDrop)` / `.absent` (server answered !exists) / `.unknown(reason)` for every throw, decode failure, and unconfigured build — defaults resolve to UNKNOWN per cross-cutting rule 1. Map FirestoreErrorCode.permissionDenied and .unauthenticated to `.unknown` with copy that does not assert a cause ('This link can't be opened right now — it may have been taken back, or your account is still connecting') plus retry; reserve the 'taken back / expired' copy for `.absent`, which only becomes producible after the v3 deploy (firestore.rules:60-64 tolerates resource == null). Gate the initial load on `account.uid != nil` (or retry once when the uid arrives) so the cold-start race stops producing a failure screen for a live link.

findings.title: The keepsake's offline recap asserts a cause it never checked and promises a landing place that does not exist — the read is one-shot and the screen is unreachable after dismissal
findings.trace: MemoryScreen.swift:74-81 renders 'Reactions land here when you're back online' for `!recap.serverAnswered`. ReactionService.swift:186-192 sets serverAnswered = false for BOTH `snapshot.metadata.isFromCache` and every thrown error (`return .unavailable` at :191, the same value as the offline case) — a permission denial, an unauthenticated read (firestore.rules.deployed:41 requires request.auth != null), or a missing index all render as 'you're offline'. The promise is also unbacked: the recap is read exactly once (`.task { recap = await reactions.reactions(for: drop) }`, MemoryScreen.swift:102) with no retry and no connectivity observer; the screen is a fullScreenCover whose dismissal calls endSession() (RootView.swift:78-81), which nils the drop (ReactionSession.swift:105-111), and there is no Memory history anywhere (ProfileScreen.swift:170 states captures 'appear here from Wave 6.2').
findings.harm: A recipient who watches a drop with no connectivity (a basement, a plane, an airport with captive wifi) is told their friends' reactions will appear on this screen once they reconnect. They reconnect; the screen has already been dismissed and can never be reopened, and no other surface shows reactions on a received drop. The one artifact the loop promises as a keepsake makes a commitment the app has no mechanism to keep — and when the real cause is a rules denial rather than connectivity, the user is also sent to debug a network that is fine.
findings.fix: Split the unknown: return a reason with ReactionRecap (`.cache` vs `.failed(Error)`), and render cache/offline as a state without a promise ('Reactions aren't loaded yet') and a failure as its own line, never as an offline claim. Back the promise or drop it — either re-run `reactions(for:)` on a retry affordance / when the recap is stale (the same `.task` keyed on a connectivity or uid change), or reword to something the mechanics can honour ('Reactions on this drop aren't loaded — reopen the drop to see them').

findings.title: Round 10's listener pruning silently kills the sender's only reaction surface for any drop that falls out of the newest-10 window — creating an 11th drop stops toasts for an older shared drop
findings.trace: ReactionService.swift:116-121 (new in round 10): `let watchedKeys = Set(mine.map(\.id.uuidString)); for (key, registration) in listeners where !watchedKeys.contains(key) { registration.remove(); listeners[key] = nil; primedListeners.remove(key) }`, where `mine = Self.watchedDrops(...)` is capped at `prefix(10)` (:81-89). Before round 10 the dictionary only grew (round-9 verdict quotes :114 with no removal loop, and stop() has no production call site), so a listener attached for a drop that later left the newest-10 kept delivering. RootView.swift:155-157 re-runs the pass on every listenKey change, and the key is exactly the watched-set identity (:97-102) — so the pruning executes the moment an 11th owned non-private drop exists. The toast (RootView.swift:101-126) is the only sender-side reaction surface: the profile counters are written by nothing (ProfileScreen.swift:55-66, UserProfile), which is the deferred ux-5 residual.
findings.harm: An active sender creates their 11th drop; the oldest shared drop's listener is torn down, and any reaction arriving on it afterwards produces no toast, no counter, no badge — it is invisible forever (the primed watermark is dropped too, so even a re-entry into the window would discard the initial snapshot). The gift the recipient did react to reads as ignored, which is the single most damaging false state for this product, and round 10 made it strictly more likely than round 9's leaking-but-delivering behaviour.
findings.fix: Separate the LISTEN set from the DISPLAY cap: prune only listeners for drops that left the LIBRARY (deleted/foreign/received), never drops that merely fell out of `prefix(10)`; i.e. compute the detach set against `drops.filter { owned && !private }` and the attach set against the capped list, or raise/remove the cap for listening and cap only what is rendered. Pair with the deferred ux-5 watermark so an un-toasted reaction still has a surface.

findings.title: For the skipped-rows incident the Dismiss affordance is a guaranteed no-op — the journal is rewritten by the refresh the dismissal itself triggers — and the ladder rung it drives claims a hold on sync that is not happening
findings.trace: LocalDropStore.loadDrops re-derives the incident on EVERY load of the same file: :202-212 writes `pendingReadWarning` and `writeIncident(message)` whenever any row fails to decode (the bad rows stay on disk — only the whole-file path quarantines/moves, :227-232). acknowledgeReadIncident (DropStore.swift:620-636) clears the journal and then calls `await self.refresh(near: nil)` at :634 (round 10, ux-3), which reloads the same file, re-journals, and re-publishes localReadWarning at :466-468. The state is also permanent for the latch: `.skippedRows` fails localProvablyClean (:561-568), so hasCompletedCleanRefresh can never be earned. Only DropsListScreen.swift:58-68 offers Dismiss; ProfileScreen.swift:103-111 shows the same condition with no affordance.
findings.harm: A user with one undecodable row in drops.json gets a banner on the Sent tab whose Dismiss button visibly does nothing (tap → banner blinks and returns), plus a permanent Profile rung reading 'Some saved drops couldn't be read — sync is on hold'. Sync is NOT on hold: add()/update() still call enqueueCloudSync (DropStore.swift:712,734) and uploads continue to ack normally. So the user is simultaneously handed an action that cannot work and a mechanism claim that is false — they may stop creating drops, or re-create drops they believe never uploaded. It self-heals only if some later save() happens to rewrite the file (save() persists the filtered array, :298-302), i.e. never for a passive user.
findings.fix: Make acknowledgement content-addressed: record the acknowledged payload digest (the same SHA256 prefix preserveUnreadable already computes, :261-264) alongside the journal, and suppress re-journaling/re-warning while the unreadable content is unchanged — a NEW failure (different digest) re-raises it. Reword the ProfileScreen rung to what is actually true ('Some saved drops couldn't be read' / 'checking' rather than 'sync is on hold'), and give ProfileScreen the same acknowledge affordance the Sent tab has so the surface that shows the state can also resolve it.

findings.title: 'FIRST IN N S' is computed over the others-only slice, so when the viewer reacted first the badge crowns someone else's later reaction
findings.trace: ReactionService.swift:182-186 builds rows as `documents (ordered by 'at') → filter !hasPendingWrites → filter uid != myUid` (the round-10 ux-2 exclusion). MemoryScreen.swift:193-198 then takes `recap.rows.first` and prints 'FIRST IN \(delta) S' from its timestamp against drop.createdAt. The viewer's own reaction — rendered with its true delivery on its own line at :59-66 — is not considered, so with two reactors where the viewer was first, the badge labels the SECOND reaction as first.
findings.harm: A fabricated superlative on the screen the product calls the keepsake: the recipient who genuinely reacted first is shown another person credited with 'FIRST IN 12 S'. Small, but it is a positive claim the data does not support, made by the exact code path round 10 changed.
findings.fix: Compute the badge over the FULL server-confirmed set (keep an `allRows` alongside the others-only `rows`, or return the earliest server-confirmed timestamp with the recap) and render 'FIRST IN N S' only when that earliest row is the one being labelled; otherwise render nothing.

findings.title: The share sheet's preview still renders the presentation-captured drop while the link payload is built from the live row — the two can describe different content
findings.trace: Round 10 (flows-3) routed `sharedDrop` through `liveDrop` (:182-191) and the retry through the id (:205), but the visible card still reads the captured value type: the map region and pin from `drop.coordinate` (:46-50), the content/scale line from `drop.content`/`drop.scale` (:75,84), and the quoted message block from `drop.message` (:114-122) — the sheet is presented with a value copy from DropsListScreen.swift:99/107 (`sharingDrop = drop`) and `library.drops` can be replaced underneath it by any refresh (DropStore.swift:527). The header chip is a hardcoded `NightChip(text: "READY")` (:41) that renders unchanged next to the terminal-failure caption at :135-143.
findings.harm: A cloud merge (or a second device's edit) while the sheet is open leaves the user reading one message/position and sending a link whose accompanying text is built from another — the sheet stops describing what it is about to send. And a drop the app already knows can never upload is still stamped READY at the top of the sheet while the caption underneath says the link won't work.
findings.fix: Render the card from `liveDrop` everywhere (`drop` should be reduced to an identity — take `let dropID: UUID` and resolve the row from the library), and derive the header chip from the same state as the caption ladder (READY only when the row is neither terminal nor pending).

cleanAreas: ProfileScreen ladder ORDER and per-rung copy (ProfileScreen.swift:78-157): each rung's string matches its predicate exactly, problems (terminal → unresolved-delete → local-read → un-pushable → sync error) correctly outrank progress, progress outranks unknown, and 'Synced' sits below the unknown rung — the ordering itself needs no change; only the reachability of the latch-gated rungs is broken (lens-1).

ReactionOverlay's delivery pill (ReactionSession.swift:227-235) — four honest states including 'Will send … when you're back online' for the queued outcome, with stale-token protection (:66-81) verified by ReactionSessionTests.swift:42.

ReceiveScreen's retry STATE MACHINE (as distinct from its verdicts): load() nils `failure` first (:145) so the ZStack falls back to the ProgressView during a retry (:36-42), and repeated failures re-render the failed view — the spinner/repeat-failure behaviour the lens asked about is complete; the defect is the verdict mapping, not the flow.

DropsListScreen banner stack (:37-79): all four failure classes render above the empty/list split, the read-incident banner carries the acknowledge affordance, and DropRow's per-row xmark.icloud (:154-159) makes the aggregate 'N can't sync' banner actionable.

Seed-failure copy (ux-7, AccountService.swift:118-126): the 'will retry on the next launch' claim is backed by the listener's server-confirmed-absence re-seed (:51,72-84), the retry is single-flight (:75-83), and a late real profile aborts the starter write (:103,107) — no fabricated success, no misdirection to connectivity.

refresh()'s two-phase publish (DropStore.swift:473-481) and the reap's tombstone-suppression skip (:536-551): a superseded refresh can now only lose the cloud half, and suppression is no longer mistaken for proof of a row's absence from disk.

findings.title: Bounded-refusal delete resolves "done" from absence of evidence — a drop whose cloud copy is owned by a previous account connection is silently reported deleted while it stays live and link-readable
findings.trace: remove() destroys the distinguishing evidence before the delete is issued: DropStore.swift:748-754 removes the row from `drops`, :752 clearPending, :753 clearTerminal (the ownedByAnotherAccount verdict), and local.delete at :742 has already erased the row (with its ownerUid) from disk. performCloudDelete then constructs a ghost carrying ONLY the id (:911-912, ownerUid nil), so FirebaseDropStore.delete's owner pre-check (:153) cannot fire and the delete is issued. Under the pinned deployed v2 ruleset (web/firestore.rules.deployed:35-36, `allow delete: if resource.data.ownerUid == request.auth.uid`) a document owned by an OLD uid denies exactly like an absent document — web/rules-tests/deployed-rules.test.mjs:53-54 pins the absent case, and the two are indistinguishable from the error alone. The catch-all at DropStore.swift:924-948 spends an attempt on ANY rejection (it does not consult DropStoreError.terminalRefusalReason, so transient gRPC 8/13/14 rejections also burn attempts), and at attempts >= 3 the verdict is chosen by `if ackedCloudIDs.contains(id)` (:943). ackedCloudIDs is written only on a save ack (:841) or a SERVER-served refresh row (:508), and the refresh query is uid-scoped (FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-66 whereField("ownerUid", isEqualTo: uid)) — so a document owned by a previous uid can never enter the set, and the set is additionally empty for every install upgrading to round 10 and every restored install. Result: the else branch at :945-947 logs "no cloud copy exists" and clears the tombstone with NO unresolvedDelete, NO surface (ProfileScreen.swift:92-102 is the only surface and keys on unresolvedDeleteIDs). This inverts binding rule 1 (the good state — 'nothing to warn about' — is reached by fallthrough) and rule 2 (a negative fact, 'the server never held this id', is asserted from a set-difference against an incomplete, default-empty durable set rather than a positive per-object check).
findings.harm: User deletes a drop whose cloud document is stamped with a previous anonymous uid (the exact population the app already models with DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount and the terminal verdict). Three refusals later the app reports the deletion complete and shows an all-clear sync ladder, while the Firestore document survives and stays readable by anyone holding the magic link (firestore.rules.deployed:30-32, visibility in ['link','public']). The sender believes they took the surprise back; the recipient can still open it, with its coordinates, message and recipient name. Same false all-clear reached by three transient (retryable) rejections, because attempts are spent without consulting the refusal taxonomy. Round 9's blocker was a permanent FALSE ALARM; round 10 traded it for a permanent FALSE ALL-CLEAR on the population where the alarm was correct.
findings.fix: Capture positive cloud-existence evidence at tombstone time, when it still exists, and key the resolution on it. In remove(), before clearTerminal, record into a durable set (e.g. `cloudProvenIDs`, defaults key `cloudProvenDropIDs`): `drop.ownerUid != nil || ackedCloudIDs.contains(drop.id) || terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id)`. `ownerUid` is non-nil ONLY when a server stamped it — grep confirms the sole writers are the ack path (DropStore.swift:853) and server reads (FirebaseDropStore.swift:73/100, DropSharingService.swift:73) — so it is a true positive per-object check and it covers upgraded/restored installs whose ackedCloudIDs is empty. performCloudDelete:943 then reads that set; absence of proof resolves to markUnresolvedDelete (visible UNKNOWN), and only a drop that was demonstrably never server-stamped and never acked resolves silently DONE. Additionally gate attempt-spending on `DropStoreError.terminalRefusalReason(error) != nil` so transient rejections keep retrying instead of consuming the budget.

findings.title: redeem() silently discards the received drop when the pending id has no live row — nothing is inserted, nothing is persisted, no error is raised
findings.trace: redeem's pending-guard returns early at DropStore.swift:679-684 on `pendingSyncIDs.contains(drop.id)` alone, before the in-memory insert (:685-689) and before local.save (:691). Its comment (:682-683) claims the row 'is already published' by the pending/tombstone invariant, but that invariant only forbids pending+tombstoned (asserts at :957-960, :983-986); it says nothing about the row existing. pending-with-no-row is a first-class modeled state — uploadingCount/unpushablePendingCount at :430-440 exist for it, and ProfileScreen.swift:112-126 renders it. It is durable across sessions: pendingSyncIDs is restored from defaults at :415-416 while the local file may have been quarantined (LocalDropStore.swift:227-241 moves the file aside) and, because post-quarantine loads report .quarantinedWholeFile then .absentFile, the reap's `if case .clean` gate (:536) never clears the orphan. Sequence: create + share (pending), local file corrupted/quarantined, relaunch → drops = [] with pendingSyncIDs = {X} → user opens their own link → ReceiveScreen fetches (DropSharingService.swift:52-83) → RootView.swift:66 calls redeem → early return → the drop is neither inserted into `drops` nor written to disk, and redeem does not throw, so RootView's catch (:67-71) never fires and no persist banner appears. RootView.swift:73-74 then starts the AR session and shows the camera on an in-memory-only value. Not covered by testRedeemNeverOverwritesAPendingLocalEdit (DropStoreTests.swift:824-853), which adds the drop first so the row always exists.
findings.harm: Silent data loss with a fabricated success: after a local-store corruption the user re-opens their own (or a friend's) magic link, watches the drop in AR for the whole session, and it is gone on the next launch — no error, no banner, no journal entry. The one situation where the fetched server copy is the ONLY surviving copy is exactly the situation in which redeem refuses to save it.
findings.fix: Make the guard test what it means to protect — a live row, not a bookkeeping flag: `if pendingSyncIDs.contains(drop.id), drops.contains(where: { $0.id == drop.id })` → return. Otherwise fall through to the insert + local.save, which restores the row from server truth (the pending id then has a loadable row again and the normal reconcile pushes it). Optionally clear the stale pending id after the restore only when the fetched copy is server-stamped.

findings.title: The own-2 two-phase publish transiently republishes the library WITHOUT its cloud-only rows, tearing down AR entities and resetting the reaction watermark the deferred seams-5 residual depends on
findings.trace: refresh() publishes `localOnly` at DropStore.swift:478-481 and then suspends on the cloud read at :490. Cloud rows are never written to disk (the merge at :504-513 has no local.save), so for any install whose local store is empty or stale relative to the cloud — the Wave 6.1 'sync MY drops across installs' case, and every post-quarantine session — phase 1 publishes a library MISSING those rows, on every refresh. Three consequences, all in-lens: (1) if the pass is superseded during the cloud read (guard at :502; add/update/remove/redeem/acknowledgeReadIncident all bump refreshGeneration at :672/:702/:720/:738/:621), refresh returns and the cloud half stays missing until the next successful refresh, which on Home/You never comes automatically. (2) RootView.swift:155-157 keys the reaction listeners on ReactionService.listenKey(for: library.drops, …) (ReactionService.swift:97-102); the phase-1 publish changes that key, SwiftUI re-runs the task during the suspension, and ReactionService.swift:116-121 (round 10's flows-5 pruning) removes the registration AND `primedListeners.remove(key)`. Phase 2 restores the key and the listener re-attaches un-primed, so its initial snapshot — with `.order(by:"at", descending:true).limit(to:1)` at :128 — is swallowed as history at :145-148. (3) GeoARSessionManager.swift:1242 feeds syncGPSPlacements from library.drops(near:within:), and :1490-1500 destroys holders, content entities, groundLockBaseY and deferred VPS transforms for every id not in the reduced set.
findings.harm: Drops that live only in the cloud (second install / post-restore / post-quarantine session) vanish from Home, Sent, Explore and the AR view mid-refresh and stay vanished if anything mutated the library during the cloud read — the user sees their drops disappear with no message and may re-create them. In AR the same rows are torn down and rebuilt on every refresh: visible pop, lost ground lock, lost VPS glide state. And the reaction toast for a reaction landing inside the detach window is discarded as history — round 10 made the deferred seams-5 watermark residual strictly more fragile by attaching pruning to an array that now churns on every refresh.
findings.fix: Do not publish a set that is knowingly incomplete. Either (a) make phase 1 additive — merge the freshly loaded local rows over the existing `drops` and apply tombstone suppression, never dropping ids the previous publish carried, and let phase 2 be the authoritative replace; or (b) persist cloud-merged rows to the local store when they are server-served, so local truth is a superset and phase 1 loses nothing. Independently, decouple the listener lifetime from a transient publish: prune a listener only after its drop has been absent from the watched set across a completed refresh (or keep primedListeners keyed by drop id beyond the registration's lifetime so a re-attach does not re-prime).

findings.title: A failed incident-journal write is indistinguishable from no incident, and the very next refresh promotes the emptied library to "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops"
findings.trace: LocalDropStore.writeIncident swallows its result — `try? Data(message.utf8).write(to: incidentNoteURL, options: .atomic)` at DropStore.swift:276-278. Round 10's lens-6 work checked the moveItem and sidecar results (:232 backedUp, :261-274 preserveUnreadable) but left the journal — the load-bearing artifact — unchecked. Trace: whole-file corruption → :227-241 quarantines the file and calls writeIncident; if that write fails (disk full, the condition most correlated with a truncated JSON write) the incident is lost, pendingReadWarning was set to nil at :234, and lastLoadReadWarning() (:286-292) returns nil. Refresh #1 still reports lastOutcome = .quarantinedWholeFile so localProvablyClean is false (:561-568 default branch). Refresh #2 — which always happens on the launch path (AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:34 then RootView.swift:164) — sees the file gone, returns .absentFile with warning nil (:180-187), so the `case .absentFile?: return localReadWarning == nil` arm at :565 evaluates TRUE, the latch is set at :570, and ProfileScreen.swift:150-157 renders 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops'. testQuarantineAbsenceEarnsNoPositiveEvidence (DropStoreTests.swift:680-699) cannot catch this: it runs in a writable tmp dir where the journal write always succeeds. Distinct from the deferred lens-2 residual (journal mirror to a second medium): the defect here is the unchecked result plus the fallthrough to the positive state, not the storage medium.
findings.harm: The exact failure the incident journal exists to make visible — a quarantine that destroyed saved drops — becomes completely silent, and the app then makes its strongest positive claim about the remains. The user sees an empty (or partial) library labelled server-confirmed, with no banner and nothing to acknowledge.
findings.fix: Make writeIncident return Bool and latch failure in the actor: on a failed journal write set a `journalWriteFailed` flag and have lastLoadOutcome()/lastLoadReadWarning() report a non-clean, non-nil result for the remainder of the process (e.g. keep lastOutcome = .quarantinedWholeFile / return a synthesized warning). localProvablyClean at DropStore.swift:561-568 then cannot evaluate true, so the run reports UNKNOWN rather than Synced — the good state stays earned rather than reached by a swallowed error.

findings.title: flows-5 releases the dead reaction registration but nothing re-attaches it — the sender's toast stays dead for the session, now with the claim that it does not
findings.trace: On a listener error ReactionService.swift:132-144 removes the registration and clears primedListeners so 'the next listen pass re-attaches'. There is no next pass: listenToMySharedDrops is called only from RootView.swift:155-157 `.task(id: ReactionService.listenKey(for: library.drops, myUid: account.uid))`, and listenKey (ReactionService.swift:97-102) is a function of the watched drop-ID set only, so an unchanged set produces an unchanged id and SwiftUI never re-runs the task body. Firestore surfaces an error on a snapshot listener only when it has given up (transient failures are retried internally without a callback), so the callback at :137-143 IS the terminal case that needs an explicit re-attach. Net behaviour is identical to pre-round-10 (dead for the session); only the code comment changed.
findings.harm: After one terminal listener error (rules change, auth blip, quota) the sender stops receiving reaction toasts for that drop for the rest of the session, with no indication. The reaction toast is the loop's payoff — the sender concludes nobody opened their drop.
findings.fix: Give the release a trigger. Track the released keys and re-attach them from an owned schedule rather than a view key: after clearing listeners[key], schedule a bounded-backoff re-attach inside ReactionService (Task + retry counter), and additionally call listenToMySharedDrops from the scenePhase == .active branch in AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:36-51 so a foreground return always repairs the set. Keep the primed watermark per drop id across the re-attach so the repair does not swallow a reaction that landed while detached.

ownFindings.title: redeem() retires a tombstone whose DELETE IS ALREADY IN FIRESTORE'S DURABLE MUTATION QUEUE — cancelling the Swift task does not recall the write, so the drop is restored locally while its cloud copy is destroyed and every shared link dies silently
ownFindings.trace: DropStore.swift:671-697 redeem(): :673 bumps deleteGenerations, :674 `deleteTasks[drop.id]?.cancel()`, :676-677 clearPendingDelete/clearUnresolvedDelete, and (by design, comment :669-670) it NEVER enqueues a cloud sync. But the delete was handed to the SDK long before: launchCloudDelete (:892-903) -> performCloudDelete (:905) -> FirebaseDropStore.delete (:147-173) -> FirestoreAcked.delete (:57-72), whose stream-build closure calls `document.delete { ... }` SYNCHRONOUSLY at FirestoreAcked.swift:62. That call enqueues a mutation in Firestore's persistent local mutation queue; the SDK exposes no recall/cancel API, and Task.cancel() only unblocks the ack wait (FirestoreAcked.swift:79-107 resolves .queuedLocally on cancellation, DropStore.swift:921-923 spends no attempt). The generation guards (:915, :936) then make the resumed task return WITHOUT clearing pendingDelete, without clearAcked(:918) — so when the queue finally flushes, nothing in the app observes it. The library's own comment at DropStore.swift:933-935 reasons about queue serialization in the opposite direction ('a staged create ... the queue serializes it before this delete') and never applies it here. After the flush the row is in `drops`, on disk (redeem :691 local.save), not pending, not terminal, not tombstoned, and still in ackedCloudIDs — every surface reads healthy.
ownFindings.harm: The headline use case of round 10's redeem() destroys the drop it is restoring. Trigger (the designed story): the user deletes a drop while offline (or with a slow ack) — the delete stages durably — then taps that drop's link in their own iMessage thread to get it back. redeem() retires the tombstone and republishes the row; minutes later the queue flushes and Firestore deletes the document. The owner now sees a normal, apparently-synced drop with no badge and no banner, while every recipient's magic link is permanently dead (under the live v2 rules the recipient's read of the absent doc DENIES, so they are shown 'You seem to be offline — the surprise may still be waiting' with an endless Try again, per the confirmed SURF-lens-2 inversion). A later delete of the same row is refused (absent doc denies under v2), the id is still in ackedCloudIDs, so it lands in unresolvedDeleteIDs and asserts 'the cloud copy may still exist' about a copy the app itself destroyed.
ownFindings.fix: Treat 'a cloud delete was ISSUED' as durable state, not as an in-memory task. Add `private var issuedDeleteIDs: Set<UUID>` persisted alongside the other sets, marked in performCloudDelete immediately before `try await cloud.delete(ghost)` (DropStore.swift:914) and cleared on a confirmed delete (:916-918) or on a completed redemption re-upload. In redeem(), after retiring the tombstones, if `issuedDeleteIDs.contains(drop.id) && drop.receivedViaLink != true`, call `enqueueCloudSync(drop)` — the create is appended AFTER the delete in the same durable queue and Firestore serializes mutations per document, so the row is re-created and the link survives; the row also enters pendingSyncIDs, so ShareDropSheet/Profile report the honest in-flight state. For `receivedViaLink == true` rows (not ours to re-upload) the honest outcome is not silence: record the id and surface it as an UNKNOWN ('this drop may no longer be shareable'). Test: park the delete gate, redeem, release, and assert the row is re-enqueued (cloud.saved contains the id) — no existing test drives redeem() against an ISSUED delete (testRedemptionSupersedesInFlightDeleteVerdict, DropStoreTests.swift:752-787, asserts only that the stale task does not tombstone, which passes with and without this bug).

ownFindings.title: One tap on Dismiss converts a destroyed-library incident into 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops': localProvablyClean treats the ABSENCE OF A USER-DISMISSABLE STRING as positive evidence that local truth is clean, and round 10 wired the dismissal to an immediate refresh
ownFindings.trace: DropStore.swift:561-568 `localProvablyClean` — `case .absentFile?: return localReadWarning == nil`. The quarantine path moves the store file away (LocalDropStore.swift:227-232) and records the incident ONLY as a user-facing string in the `.incident` journal (:238-240, read back at :286-292). acknowledgeIncident() (:251-254) deletes that journal, and round 10's ux-3 change (DropStore.swift:620-636) makes acknowledgeReadIncident() immediately `await self.refresh(near: nil)` at :634. That refresh reloads: the file is gone -> LocalDropStore.swift:180-187 returns `.absentFile` with `pendingReadWarning = nil`, lastLoadReadWarning() is now nil, so localReadWarning is nil (DropStore.swift:466-468) -> localProvablyClean == true -> with a server-served cloud read the latch is set at :569-571 -> ProfileScreen.swift:150-157 renders 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops'. The durable evidence that the store WAS quarantined survives on disk as `drops.json.corrupt-<timestamp>` (LocalDropStore.swift:227-232) and as the `.unreadable-<digest>` sidecars (:261-274) and is never consulted by any load or by the latch. FLOWS-lens-5 found the same landing zone via a swallowed writeIncident failure (:276-278); this path needs no failure at all — it is the designed acknowledgement flow, and round 10's own-1 change made acknowledgement the ONLY way to retire the journal (:216-219), so every user with a quarantine incident is routed through it.
ownFindings.harm: A user whose drops.json was quarantined sees the honest banner, taps the Dismiss button the app offers (DropsListScreen.swift:66-68), and the very next screen state is the app's strongest positive claim over a library that just lost rows. Drops that were received via link are the concrete loss: they are never enqueued for cloud sync (DropStore.swift:809), so they are never in pendingSyncIDs and never in the uid-scoped cloud read — after the quarantine they exist nowhere, the ux-4 un-pushable rung cannot see them, and after one tap the app asserts server confirmation of a library they are missing from. The acknowledgement of a MESSAGE is being read as acknowledgement of CLEANLINESS.
ownFindings.fix: Separate the incident's user-facing lifecycle from the store's machine-checkable cleanliness. (1) Give LocalDropStore a durable, non-dismissable quarantine marker: on load, if any `drops.json.corrupt-*` or `drops.json.unreadable-*` artifact exists next to the store, an `.absentFile`/`.clean` outcome must be downgraded — return `.quarantinedWholeFile`-equivalent or expose `everQuarantined: Bool` on LocalStoreDiagnostics — so `localProvablyClean` (DropStore.swift:561-568) keys on a fact the user cannot dismiss. This also closes FLOWS-lens-5: a failed moveItem leaves the original file in place, so the next load is not `.absentFile` either way, and a failed writeIncident no longer matters to the latch. (2) Make acknowledgeIncident() retire only the BANNER, recording the acknowledged digest, never the cleanliness verdict. (3) Test: quarantine a file, refresh, acknowledgeReadIncident(), refresh with a server-served GatedCloudStore, assert `!library.hasCompletedCleanRefresh` — testQuarantineAbsenceEarnsNoPositiveEvidence (DropStoreTests.swift:680-699) never acknowledges, so it passes with and without this bug.

VERDICTS RESTING ON UNVERIFIED PLATFORM ASSUMPTIONS: (1) My REFUTATION of SEAMS-lens-2's harm rests on Firestore's permanent-vs-retryable write-error classification (isPermanentWriteError: UNAVAILABLE / RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED / INTERNAL / DEADLINE_EXCEEDED / UNAUTHENTICATED are retried inside the SDK and never reach the write completion). If the mutation were somehow recallable, own-A collapses to an ordering nit.
